content: 1. Counsel patients on the importance of consuming iron-rich foods to support their health during pregnancy and postpartum. Provide specific examples of such foods and their benefits. 2. If a patient is taking both calcium and iron supplements, advise them to take these at different times of the day, such as calcium in the morning and iron in the evening, to optimize absorption and efficacy. 3. Administer iron and folic acid supplements routinely to all pregnant, postpartum, and post-abortion women. This should be done daily during pregnancy and for three months after delivery or abortion. For women with anemia, provide a double dose (twice daily). 4. At each visit, check the patient’s supply of iron and folic acid tablets and dispense a three-month supply as needed. Advise them to store the tablets safely, away from children and in a dry place. 5. Educate patients and their families about the importance of iron for maternal health during pregnancy and after delivery. Explain the risks of anemia and the necessity of supplementation. Address any misconceptions, such as fears that iron will cause excessive bleeding or lead to a large baby. 6. Discuss potential side effects of iron supplements, such as constipation or nausea, and provide strategies to manage them. For example, suggest drinking more water for constipation or taking the tablets after meals or at night to reduce nausea. Reassure patients that these side effects are not serious and encourage them to return if they experience difficulties. 7. If necessary, involve family members, traditional birth attendants, or community health workers in promoting the use of iron and folate tablets. 8. Counsel patients on the use of insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria. Confirm whether the patient and newborn will sleep under a bed net, and if so, check when it was last treated with insecticide. Advise re-treatment every six months. 9. For malaria prevention during pregnancy, administer sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine as per national guidelines during antenatal visits in the second and third trimesters. Ensure the last dose was given within the past month; if not, provide three tablets under direct observation. Inform the patient when the next dose is due and monitor the baby for jaundice if the medication is given close to delivery. 10. Do not administer sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine to HIV-infected pregnant women receiving cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Instead, follow alternative malaria prevention protocols. 11. For antimalarial treatment, consider artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) known to be effective in the region. Alternatively, use artesunate plus clindamycin or quinine plus clindamycin for seven days. Avoid dapsone, primaquine, or tetracycline in lactating women. 12. Provide paracetamol for severe pain, with a dosage of 500 mg per tablet. Advise taking 1–2 tablets every 4–6 hours as needed. 13. For bacterial infections, prescribe appropriate antibiotics based on the condition. For example: Mastitis: Cloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days. Lower urinary tract infection: Amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours for 3 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 80 mg/400 mg every 12 hours for 3 days. Avoid these in late pregnancy and during breastfeeding. Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly for the woman and ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally for the partner (not safe for pregnant or lactating women). Chlamydia: Erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 7 days for the woman. For the partner, use tetracycline or doxycycline (not safe for pregnant or lactating women). Trichomonas or bacterial vaginosis: Metronidazole 2 g as a single dose or 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 days. Avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy. 14. Before administering penicillin, rule out any history of allergy. After injection, observe the patient for signs of an allergic reaction, such as chest tightness, swelling, rash, or difficulty breathing. If an allergic reaction occurs, manage it immediately by opening the airway, administering IV fluids, and giving adrenaline as needed. 15. Provide tetanus toxoid immunization to all women due for their dose. Check their immunization status and plan subsequent doses as per the WHO-recommended schedule. Explain that the vaccine is safe during pregnancy and will not harm the baby. Record the immunization on the mother’s card. 16. For women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, administer low-dose aspirin (75 mg daily) from 12 weeks of pregnancy until delivery. In areas with low dietary calcium intake, provide calcium supplements (1500 mg daily) throughout pregnancy. 17. Administer mebendazole (500 mg) to all women once every six months, except during the first trimester of pregnancy. 18. Counsel patients on the correct and consistent use of condoms to prevent sexually transmitted infections. Provide information on HIV, including its transmission, prevention, and treatment options. 19. For women allergic to penicillin, prescribe erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 15 days. If the partner is allergic to penicillin, use tetracycline or doxycycline (not safe for pregnant or lactating women). 20. Always ensure that preventive measures and treatments are tailored to the patient’s specific needs, considering their medical history, pregnancy status, and any potential contraindications.
